passage.title: What Leaders Are Made Of
paras: Studies of effective leaders keep returning to a handful of qualities: honesty, fairness, self-control, courage and care for the people they serve. Notice what is missing from the list: fear. Leaders who rule through fear may be obeyed, but they are rarely trusted, and power without trust is fragile. When it cracks, it cracks all at once.

Fear works quickly. A threat can make people do what they are told by the end of the day. But it also teaches them to hide mistakes, to tell the leader only what the leader wants to hear, and to wait for the moment when the threat is gone. A leader surrounded by frightened people is a leader who no longer knows what is really happening.

Trust is slower to build. It grows when a leader keeps promises, applies the same rules to friends and rivals, admits errors and protects the weakest people in their care. Once built, it is remarkably strong: people will follow a trusted leader through hardship because they believe the hardship is shared and the purpose is good.

History offers both kinds. Some rulers held power for years through spies and punishment, only to be abandoned overnight when their armies refused to fight. Others, with far less force, were followed with loyalty that outlived them.

The lesson for any leader, from a head of state to a team captain, is the same. You can make people afraid of you, or you can make them believe in you. Only one of those will hold when the storm comes.
